props.title: 12 Angry Lebanese
props.initialSlug: Passion on trial. Justice at stake.

sections.content: **12 Angry Lebanese (2009)** (2009) revolutionizes the intersection of prison reform and theater documentation. Director Zeina Daccache adapts Reginald Rose's 12 Angry Men (1957) inside Roumieh Prison, Lebanon's largest male prison, transforming inmates into actors. This groundbreaking documentary echoes similar prison arts initiatives like **Shakespeare Behind Bars** (2005) and **The Acting Class** (2017), but stands apart through its raw Middle Eastern context and the profound personal transformations captured on screen. movies.title: 12 Angry Men
movies.slug: The original courtroom drama that inspired the Lebanese adaptation, following 12 jurors deliberating a murder case

sections.content: The documentary's power lies in its parallel narratives - the inmates' personal journeys mirror the transformation of their theatrical characters. Like **The Act of Killing** (2012), which had perpetrators reenact their crimes through cinema, **12 Angry Lebanese** uses performance as both therapy and confession. The inmates grapple with their own prejudices and crimes while embodying characters who must overcome similar biases.

The film's impact extends beyond its prison walls, challenging Lebanese society's views on rehabilitation. Similar to **Carandiru** (2003), which exposed Brazil's prison system through dramatization, Daccache's documentary sparked national dialogue about incarceration reform. The success of this program led to further arts initiatives in Middle Eastern prisons, documented in follow-up projects like **Scheherazade's Diary** (2013). sections.content: The film's unique approach to rehabilitation through theater builds on a tradition seen in documentaries like **Every Little Step** (2008) and **Anna Deavere Smith: Notes from the Field** (2018). What sets **12 Angry Lebanese** apart is its focus on masculinity and justice in the Arab world, where such programs are rare. The inmates' transformation through performance recalls **The Shawshank Redemption** (1994), but with the added weight of documentary reality.
